Multifamily SEO Services: What Should Be Included and How to Judge Them

Nov 2, 2026Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM5 min read
Key takeaways
  • Good multifamily SEO is judged by whether renters who do not know your name can find you, on Google Search, Google Maps and in AI answers.
  • Ranking for your own community name proves very little, because the renter already knew you.
  • Expect website answers to renter questions, Google Business Profile care, Maps measurement, a review program, AI answer checks and clear reporting.
  • Be wary of guaranteed rankings or a universal timeline. Google itself says no one can guarantee a #1 ranking.
In this article
  1. Why is apartment SEO its own job?
  2. What should be included?
  3. What should make you wary?
  4. How do you judge whether it is working?

Multifamily SEO services should make your community easier to find for renters who do not yet know your name, across Google Search, Google Maps and increasingly AI answers. If the work and the reporting cannot show movement on those unbranded searches, you are paying for activity.

That is a higher bar than most proposals set. A common apartment SEO line covers a monthly audit, a few blog posts and a rankings report full of terms you were already winning. I would ask for more.

Why is apartment SEO its own job?

A community is a single place competing with others inside a few miles, and renters often begin without a name in mind. In an Apartments.com survey reported by the National Apartment Association, 87% of more than 15,000 adults planning to rent had no specific property in mind when they started. Your name will usually rank. That tells you very little.

In one audit of a newly opened community, branded visibility was strong while unbranded local terms sat on pages 2 to 6. A report built on the first half of that sentence would have looked great. Our earlier post on why apartment SEO is different goes further into how this has shifted.

What should be included?

Here is the scope I would expect, written as outcomes. How a team gets there is the part you are paying them for.

  • A site that answers renter questions. Pets, fees, parking, lease terms, specials and floor plans, stated clearly and consistently on pages search engines can read. We call this work the Answer Layer. Many property sites hide those answers in widgets or PDFs, and Google says a page must be indexed to appear as a supporting link in its AI features.
  • A Google Business Profile that someone owns. Facts, photos, categories and policy compliance checked by a person. Google says complete and accurate information makes a business easier to match with the right searches, and it weighs relevance, distance and prominence.
  • Maps visibility measured where renters are. A rank checked from the leasing office tells you little. You want to see where you hold ground and where you vanish across the trade area. See how operators win in Google Maps.
  • A review program. Google says more reviews and positive ratings can help local ranking, and that replying shows you value feedback. Ask how the team encourages reviews and who writes the replies.
  • A check on AI answers. What ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity say about you, whether it is accurate, and where errors come from.
  • A named fix list for your web team. Many property sites run on a platform your agency cannot edit directly. Good SEO service includes exact requests for whoever controls the site, and tracks them until they are done.

You will notice blog posts are missing. We stopped writing them for client communities because we did not see them earn their place. A renter choosing an apartment rarely needs a generic article on your site, and the budget works harder on the answers above. Reasonable people disagree, so ask any vendor to show you which of its posts earned tours.

What should make you wary?

Guarantees

Google's advice is direct: "No one can guarantee a #1 ranking on Google." It also warns against SEOs who claim a "special relationship" with Google.

Page volume sold as progress

Fifty neighborhood pages with the same paragraph and a swapped place name look busy on an invoice. Google's spam policies describe doorway abuse as pages created to rank for specific, similar searches, and scaled content abuse as many pages generated mainly to manipulate rankings. If a proposal counts pages, ask what each page would tell a renter that no other page does.

AI content nobody read

Google's October 2026 guidance calls for fact checking AI generated content by hand, and that includes titles, meta descriptions and alt text. A wrong pet fee in a page title is still wrong. Ask who reviewed it.

A report with no dates and no misses

Every number should state the period it covers, and some months should include something that did not work. Rising impressions with no comment on actions taken deserve a follow up question. Also check the labels. A Call button tap is a tap, and it does not prove a conversation took place.

Fixes copied from a template

"Add an FAQ" is a poor recommendation if your site already has one. Before anyone suggests a change, they should have read your live site and be able to quote what it says now. We hold ourselves to that rule on every recommendation.

How do you judge whether it is working?

Ask for these on one page, by community, with dates:

  1. How often you appear for searches that do not include your name, and the trend.
  2. Where you stand on Maps across your trade area compared with your true competitors.
  3. Actions from your Google profile, such as direction requests, website clicks and Call button taps, labeled for what they are.
  4. What AI tools say about you, and whether it is right.
  5. What changed this period, and what is next.

Be careful reading declines too. Fewer appearances does not prove fewer renters were searching, and one good week is not a trend. Google suggests asking any SEO "What kind of results do you expect to see, and in what timeframe?" Get that answer in writing at the start, since the honest version will depend on your competition and your starting point.

This is the thinking behind LocalLift and the Weekly Pulse: one read for each community, with each number dated and one next step. Our multifamily marketing agency page explains how it connects with social and paid media.

Questions we hear

What do multifamily SEO services include?

At minimum, website answers to renter questions, Google Business Profile management, Maps measurement, a review program, AI answer checks and clear reporting. Blog volume alone is not a plan.

How long does apartment SEO take to show results?

It depends on your competition and starting point, so be wary of a universal promise. Ask for an expected timeframe in writing, and ask what early signs you should see before leases move.

Is SEO worth it for a stabilized community?

Usually, since unbranded visibility reduces how much you depend on ads and listing sites. The case gets stronger if you can see which searches you are missing today.

Is multifamily SEO different from AI visibility?

They overlap. AI features in Google draw on indexed pages, while other tools can name different communities. We measure both, because ranking on one does not guarantee the other.

Should the rankings report be our main measure?

No. Rankings for your own name say little. Look at unbranded appearances, Maps coverage and profile actions, and tie them to tours where you can.
